analysis.one_liner: Moves TSA screeners and air marshals onto the standard federal pay, benefits, and union system.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 137 cosponsors — 125 Democrats and 12 Republicans — but never received a committee markup or a House vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: TSA security officers, Federal air marshals, and inspectors work under a separate personnel system created after 9/11, in which the agency sets their pay, benefits, and workplace rules outside the normal federal civil-service framework. This bill would convert them to the standard federal system, giving them full collective bargaining rights, grievance and appeal protections, standard overtime and availability pay, and a guarantee of no cut in pay during the switch. It also requires reports on assaults against TSA workers and on harassment in the workplace.
analysis.who_benefits: TSA screeners, Federal air marshals, and transportation security inspectors, who would gain collective bargaining rights, standard federal benefits and appeals, guaranteed overtime and availability pay, and protection against any pay reduction during the conversion.

how_it_helps.text: Within 90 days of enactment, federal civil-service chapters 71 and 77 — covering collective bargaining and disciplinary appeals — would apply to employees performing screening functions, and they would remain eligible to form a collective bargaining unit, with bargaining at the national level.

Converted employees could not have their pay reduced, would be credited for service in TSA pay bands as if served in equivalent General Schedule grades, and air marshals would keep law enforcement availability pay and overtime at least equal to Fair Labor Standards Act rates.

The Office of Personnel Management would have to create proper position classifications for Transportation Security Officers, air marshals, and inspectors, and pending grievances could move into the standard federal appeal system or be preserved until those rights apply.

The bill directs annual reports on workforce morale and retention, a briefing on assaults and threats against screeners by members of the public, and a Comptroller General review of harassment and assault protections for TSA staff.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would bear the cost of bringing TSA workers up to standard federal pay and benefit structures; the bill authorizes appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary.' TSA management would also lose its separate authority to set personnel policy unilaterally.

drawbacks.text: The conversion would be administratively heavy: OPM must build new classification standards and the federal payroll system must be retooled on fixed deadlines, creating a risk of disruption during a transition for a security-critical workforce.

During the transition, TSA could not modify its existing personnel system except for pay-parity adjustments, new policy reported to Congress, or emerging security threats — a constraint on management flexibility that supporters argued was needed to lock in current worker protections.
The bill carries no cost estimate and authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary,' leaving the taxpayer cost of aligning TSA pay and benefits with the standard federal system open-ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — putting a large federal security workforce under the same union, appeal, and pay protections as the rest of the civil service, with no pay cut — is real and was broadly popular across both parties. The costs are the open-ended appropriation and the risk of administrative disruption during conversion; the bill tries to manage that with transition rules, preserved grievances, and exceptions for security threats, though a rushed conversion remained a genuine hazard.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and a subcommittee in May 2024; neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the term ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bennie Thompson introduced the bill on May 14, 2024, with 15 original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, the House referred it to the Homeland Security Committee and the Oversight and Accountability Committee, and it was sent to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security.
It attracted 137 cosponsors — 125 of 216 House Democrats and 12 of 224 House Republicans — but no committee held a markup and the House never voted on it.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: TSA management keeps the separate personnel system it can adjust without standard civil-service constraints, and the TSA workforce remains outside the federal framework most federal employees have. The House committees that held the bill avoided a floor vote on a measure with bipartisan backing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TSA management and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Bennie G. Thompson
for.role: Ranking Member, House Committee on Homeland Security
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 15 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 12 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 8 of the 15 original cosponsors.

for.name: American Federation of Government Employees
for.role: Labor union certified in 2011 as the representative for TSA screening agents
for.what_they_did: Advocated for years to bring TSA workers under standard federal collective bargaining rights; the bill names the union certified on June 29, 2011 as the exclusive representative for screening agents.

against.name: House Committee on Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Transportation and Maritime Security Subcommittee and took no further action; no markup was ever held.

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at sponsorship — 125 of 216 Democrats and 12 of 224 Republicans signed on — but the Republican-controlled committees that held the bill never brought it to a vote, so no roll call was ever taken.

industries.industry: Federal labor organizations representing TSA workers
industries.note: The bill would make union representation and national-level collective bargaining permanent statutory rights for screening agents rather than agency-granted privileges under a directive that a future administration could change. Union membership in this workforce would gain enforceable bargaining rights.

The agency would lose its standalone authority to set pay, benefits, and personnel policy for its workforce, though the bill preserves exceptions for emerging security threats and keeps the Administrator's flexibility on premium pay. Travelers share an interest in a stable, well-staffed security workforce.

industries.industry: Air travelers and the airline industry
industries.note: A more stable, better-protected screener workforce could improve retention at checkpoints that the airline industry depends on, while any added federal personnel costs flow through general appropriations rather than ticket prices. The bill's provisions for this group are indirect.
